source.title: Navigating Scaling Laws: Accelerating Vision Transformer's Training via Adaptive Strategies
source.authors: Sotiris Anagnostidis; Gregor Bachmann; Imanol Schlag; Thomas Hofmann

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper is present. Some figures and tables are flattened, but the relevant results are identifiable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out validation loss for language models across context-length settings and investigates scaling-based scheduling; it also extends compute-scaling experiments to vision models and downstream image performance.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own language-model test-loss curves and vision-model performance results, which are included below. Claims and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Numerous additional fixed-patch-size and model-size curves appear in the figures and appendices; only representative conditions are retained, with omissions noted below.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a method paper: it schedules shape parameters (patch size, context size, width) along fitted scaling curves. Along the way it reports its own fixed-shape ViT curves, ImageNet-1k 10-shot error vs FLOPs (about 1e16–1e19) with saturating power laws E=a(C+d)^-b+c fitted to empirical points (Fig 4, 8, 10, 15). That bears on V5, the power-law form beyond text pretraining. The LM part (Fig 9) is a single 138M model's loss-vs-FLOPs curve per context size, with no fit or fit quality reported, so it cannot show V1's power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that adapting shape parameters during training (patch size, context length, width, batch size, objective) to follow the steepest fitted scaling curve outperforms static models in compute efficiency: up to about 60% fewer FLOPs for ViTs and 40% for LM context scheduling. They expect the largest gains early, and no better infinite-compute performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies scaling-law fits to vision downstream error and language-model validation loss, then uses them to schedule patch size, context size, width, and training choices. It does not reproduce the original language-model parameter/token scaling experiments or the compute-optimal parameter/token allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on patch size and context size, which have different efficient regions at different compute levels. The paper also notes that hyperparameter choices can change with larger compute budgets and that learning-rate scheduling could shift results.

fits_no_version.finding: Error is not monotonic in patch size: patch 6 gives small gains at very high cost, and patch 4 has a worse asymptote c_P than larger patches (Fig 8, V256-6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Resolution or tokenization shape parameters, unlike size and data, have an optimum beyond which the asymptotic error worsens.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling curves for different patch sizes, context sizes, widths, batch sizes and objectives cross. Switching along the steepest curve saves up to 40% (LM context) to 60% (ViT patch) of FLOPs to reach equal performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive shape schedules informed by fitted scaling curves beat static compute-optimal models in training compute.

record.problems: Most plotted curves and values are not tabulated and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The language-model experiments use one embedding dimension and depth, and validation examples are truncated to each context size; the authors note that longer contexts are expected to have lower test loss because they provide more context. The authors also state that hyperparameters were selected using a small compute budget and that optimal choices could change at larger budgets.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other fixed patch-size curves and additional ViT model classes from Figures 4, 8, 14, and Appendix C, as well as width-scaling and scheduling curves in Figures 10–11 and 16. The paper reports many such plotted settings; representative V640-12 conditions and the central scheduled result are retained rather than exceeding the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No sweep of parameter count. LM loss vs tokens is shown only for one 138M model, with no fit reported.
No test of extrapolating small-run fits to much larger runs.
No parameter/token compute-optimal allocation analysis for LMs. A ViT compute-optimal frontier (Fig 6, Fig 20) exists but gives no allocation exponents.
Depth/width at fixed parameter count is not studied. Patch size changes compute and performance strongly but is not a fixed-parameter shape comparison in V4's sense.
No LM downstream tasks and no mapping from pretraining loss to task performance. ViT few-shot transfer is treated under V5.
No comparison of fitting methods or setups. Fits use a Huber loss, no LR schedule or cooldown, and hyperparameters tuned at 4e17 FLOPs; the effect of these choices is not tested.

missing.what: Width/model-size scaling curves at fixed patch 20 for V192-12 to V768-12, with fitted power laws; different widths are optimal at different compute.
IsoFLOP curves and the compute-optimal static frontier across model size and patch size; larger models and smaller patches are favoured as FLOPs grow.
Fitted scaling laws for all six other ViT classes across patch sizes.
Additional downstream metrics (ImageNet, Pets, Birds, 5/10-shot) vs FLOPs for V384-12.

record.verdict_notes: Primarily a method paper that uses scaling-law fits as a tool. Only the fixed-shape ViT curves bear on a version (V5). The compute axis is samples seen within single runs with constant LR and no cooldown, which the authors flag as a limitation. LM validation is truncated per context size, so loss is not comparable across contexts. Rows R7 and R8 have the wrong subject (V256-6).

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss against compute for language models with fixed architecture and several context sizes. It does not sweep parameter count or independently vary training-token count while holding other factors fixed.
No test of whether fits on small runs predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not vary parameter count and training-token count to measure their compute-optimal allocation as a function of compute.
The architecture experiments report downstream image error, not the loss named in this version; no direct test of loss sensitivity to depth, width, or architecture details is reported.
Tests vision-model scaling using ImageNet downstream error and explores context length in language-model training. Does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests downstream image performance against compute. Does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
Does not compare alternative fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, or training schedules to establish dependence of exponents or allocation trends on such choices.

rows.subject: V640-12
rows.operation_detail: Measured ImageNet-1k 10-shot error against compute for a fixed patch size.
rows.note: The authors state that some absolute performance gains remain at patch size 6, though the additional compute required is extremely high.
rows.check: Subject is wrong: Fig 8 trains V256-6 (5.1M params), not V640-12 (60M). The curve is still fitted by the power-law form. Small gains at patch 6 concern the patch-size effect, not scaling form.

rows.subject: V640-12

rows.check: Subject is wrong: V256-6, not V640-12. The non-monotonicity (patch 4 has a worse asymptote c_P) is about patch size, not about whether error follows a power law in compute. 'Partial' is misapplied to V5.

relationships.condition: ViTs (V256-6, V640-12) pre-trained on ImageNet-21k at 120px with fixed patch sizes; ImageNet-1k 10-shot error vs FLOPs, about 1e16–1e19
relationships.reason: The saturating power law a(C+d)^-b+c is fitted to empirical points for each patch size (R5–R8). Fit quality is not quantified, and the curves come from runs without LR cooldown.
relationships.display_finding: Few-shot error fit a(C+d)^−b+c for each patch size in runs without learning-rate cooldown.
